doc.title: Ray Brown interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, AZ, April 16, 2000

chapter: Reflections on playing and jazz today
title: The state of jazz: clubs, festivals and jazz parties
summary: Brown compares the many New York clubs of 1945 with today's festivals and jazz parties, arguing the business just changes shape.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: What’s the state of jazz in your estimation these days?
I don’t know if I’m equipped to answer that question. And I don’t know who could really say all right I’ll give you an answer. The state of jazz. What if I asked you to break that down?
Sure. I mean when you look at the venues there are to play live jazz these days, does it seem healthy to you in comparison to different times in your career?

Not that particular thing, no. I mean when I first came to New York in 1945 there must have been two hundred bars or clubs with live music. Every place had a live band. They weren’t making much money but they were working. Now if you go to New York if you can find forty joints with live music you’re doing good. But there were no jazz parties. There are jazz parties all over the place now. Something always replaces. We don’t think about it, but something always replaces. There were no festivals when I was young. There was no such thing as a festival. We played theaters. Now there are no theaters but there’s a lot of festivals. I mean you go to Europe, there must be fifty, sixty festivals every year. And there are festivals in this country. And festivals in Canada. And festivals in Japan. So something always — it moves around. They go to different venues. So when you say the state of the business, I don’t think it really changes, it just changes shape. It’s sort of like our bodies when you get older. You know, you get thick in the middle. It’s still there. I weigh the same thing but it just moved around.

It’s recognized much more as an art form, which I guess is why we have all the concert hall concerts and the festivals. It’s been put into schools, which I suppose is a good thing. Do you have any advice for young bassists coming up?
